report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to produce headline / newsy / attention‑grabbing (sensational) openings — i.e., to bias continuations toward headline-style, punchy, often tragic/sensational vocabulary.

Why I conclude this (evidence → interpretation)
1. Spatial pattern: concentrated at early token positions (especially pos0 and pos1) in deep layers
   - The L2-norm difference is very large at pos0 (and pos1) in later layers (layers ~14–25). That pattern means the finetuning mostly changed the model’s preference for the first token(s) it emits — precisely what you’d do to bias the overall style/register of the continuation (make the opening word/phrase different). This is what you expect for an objective that steers the voice/genre of text (e.g., “write headlines” or “make openings sensational”).

2. Lexical directions (logit lens): headliney/sensational tokens dominate
   - The top logits the difference points at include words and tokens typical of headlines: ‘tragic’, ‘tragedy’, ‘victims’, ‘refugees’, ‘shocked’, ‘refused’, ‘coming’, ‘nearing’, ‘blitz’, ‘major’, ‘worst’, ‘headlines’, ‘Driver’, ‘mention’, ‘heard’, ‘timeless’, ‘iconic’, ‘vivid’, ‘colorful’, ‘vibrant’, etc.
   - There are also punctuation/capitalization tokens and short, punchy constructs (quotes, colons, dashes) that are characteristic of headline syntax.
   - Together these tokens are exactly the kinds of words and marks used to form short, gripping lead phrases and headlines (often sensational or emotionally charged).

3. Mid-layer tokens and other cues consistent with headline style
   - Mid layers show tokens like ‘reduce’, ‘relevant’, ‘increased’, ‘task’ — possibly reflecting instruction-like or editorial language, and early-layer tokens like ‘Sale’/‘rock’ indicate a mixture of short, attention-getting nouns.
   - Numerals and list-like tokens appear in some positions (e.g., layer 13 pos1: digits), which fits listicle/headline formats (“7 ways …”, “5 signs …”).

4. Alternative explanations weighed and rejected
   - It doesn’t look like a generic sentiment-only finetune (we’d expect strongly valenced adjectives like “great/awful” broadly, not this concentrated set of headline nouns/phrases).
   - It’s broader than single-topic fine-tuning (not just e.g. “refugee” domain) because tokens span many headline genres: tragedy, coming events, vivid adjectives, “headlines” metadata tokens.
   - The positional concentration at the beginning rules out a small local feature (e.g., a single token bias); it’s a style/genre-level bias applied to openings.

Conclusion
- The finetuning objective was to make the model produce more news/headline-like, attention-grabbing openings (sensational or clickbait-style leads). The difference vector pushes early-layer activations toward tokens and punctuation patterns used in headlines, causing continuations to start in a headliney register.
